country.comment: The study analyzes municipally-owned water utilities across the United States using national American Water Works Association survey data and six U.S. geographical regions (with state-level regulation noted in Maine, Indiana, Montana, West Virginia, and Wisconsin).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Section I; PDF p. 4, Section II and Table 1; PDF p. 11, Note 9

effect_estimate.comment: Both state-regulated and locally-regulated municipal water utilities priced residential water above estimated long-run marginal cost, but state PUC regulation was associated with statistically significantly lower deadweight monopoly welfare loss as a share of residential water bills (Table 2 notes -4.6 percentage points in Model 1, which corresponds to 9.6% vs. 5.2% with rounding, and -4.24 percentage points in Model 2 for 10.39% vs. 6.15%).
effect_estimate.value: Deadweight monopoly welfare loss as a percentage of residential customers' annual water revenue/bill was significantly lower for state-regulated municipal water utilities (n = 27) than for locally-regulated municipal water utilities (n = 88): in Model 1 (unweighted utility mean), welfare loss averaged 5.2% (SE = 0.818) for state-regulated utilities versus 9.6% (SE = 0.583) for locally-regulated utilities (difference = -4.6 percentage points, or 46% lower; t-ratio = -4.58, p < 0.01 one-tailed); in Model 2 (weighted by average residential water bill size), welfare loss averaged 6.15% (SE = 1.35) for state-regulated utilities versus 10.39% (SE = 0.786; reported as 10.4% in text) for locally-regulated utilities (difference = -4.24 percentage points, or 41% lower; t-ratio = -2.71, p < 0.01 one-tailed).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 8, Table 2; PDF pp. 8-10, Section IV

mechanism_certainty.comment: Cross-sectional observational study capped at ceiling 2; assigned 1 (documented statistical association) because the paper tests cross-sectional differences in estimated price-cost welfare loss between state-regulated and locally-regulated municipal utilities without directly observing regulatory rate-review proceedings or administrative tariff-setting mechanisms.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 2, Section I; PDF p. 4, Section II; PDF pp. 8-9, Table 2 and Section IV

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines residential monopoly water pricing/rate structures exceeding long-run marginal cost as a consumer exaction (BURDEN, fees) and tests whether regulatory review of municipal utility rate structures by state public utility commissions versus local city councils/water commissions constrains monopoly pricing (ENFORCEMENT, administrative_review).
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 1-2, Abstract and Section I; PDF pp. 8-9, Table 2 and Section IV; PDF p. 11, Note 9

outcome_flags.comment: Measures residential water bills/tariffs relative to long-run marginal cost and consumer deadweight loss as a percentage of annual residential water bills (affordability), constructed from residential consumption quantities and estimated demand reductions from monopoly pricing (service_quantity).

sample_size.comment: Utilities were included from the 1965 American Water Works Association Survey of Operating Data (matched with 1960 AWWA water bill prices for demand elasticities) based on data completeness for each estimation step.
sample_size.value: 115 municipally-owned water utilities in the welfare loss comparison (88 locally-regulated utilities and 27 state-regulated utilities); 95 municipally-owned utilities in the total variable cost and distribution loss regressions; 87 utilities in the total fixed cost regression
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 5, Section III; PDF p. 6, Section III; PDF p. 7, Section III; PDF p. 8, Table 2

study_design.comment: Uses cross-sectional utility operating data from the 1965 AWWA survey (and 1960 AWWA survey prices with Foster and Beattie regional price elasticity parameters) to estimate utility-specific long-run marginal costs and deadweight monopoly welfare losses, comparing state-regulated (5 states) and locally-regulated municipal utilities.
study_design.value: Cross-sectional observational econometric study (ordinary least squares cost and distribution-loss regressions combined with regional demand elasticities and two-group difference-in-means t-tests)
study_design.where_found: PDF pp. 3-8, Sections II-IV and Table 2
